title: Blood Moon Alert: August's Sturgeon Moon Will Slip Into a Deep Eclipse
summary: Mark your calendars: the night of August 27–28 will deliver a celestial spectacle as the full Sturgeon Moon undergoes a deep partial lunar eclipse. At its maximum, 96% of the moon will be draped in Earth's dark inner shadow, transforming it into a haunting blood-red orb. The eclipse will be visible across the Americas, much of Europe, and Africa. In the United States, the moon rises at sunset on August 27. Observers on the West Coast will see Earth's shadow already darkening the lunar disk as it climbs above the horizon, while those on the East Coast must wait a few hours after sunset for the umbral silhouette to appear. The moon may initially glow yellow-orange due to Rayleigh scattering — the same effect that paints sunsets in warm hues. It may also appear larger near the horizon, a trick of perception known as the Moon Illusion. As the eclipse progresses, the moon will slide deeper into Earth's umbra. At peak, only a thin silvery crescent will remain untouched, while the rest glows an eerie red. This color comes from sunlight refracted through Earth's atmosphere; blue wavelengths are scattered away, leaving only the red light to reach the lunar surface. The August full moon is traditionally called the Sturgeon Moon by Native American tribes, referencing the giant fish readily caught in the Great Lakes at this time. Other names include the Flying Up Moon (Cree), Corn Moon, and Harvest Moon. The eclipse also coincides with the Hindu festival of Raksha Bandhan, celebrating sibling bonds. Beyond the moon, the Summer Triangle — Vega, Deneb, and Altair — will shine overhead, while Venus glimmers low in the west. Spica, the brightest star in Virgo, will appear near the moon before setting. The eclipse's peak occurs at 12:18 a.m. EDT on August 28. Whether you're a seasoned stargazer or a casual observer, this is a must-see event.
why_it_matters: Lunar eclipses like this one are rare free spectacles that connect us to both scientific understanding of orbital mechanics and cultural traditions spanning centuries.

background_read: Lunar eclipses have mesmerized skywatchers since ancient times. When the Earth aligns directly between the sun and moon, its shadow falls on the lunar surface, often tinting it red.

This eerie color arises from Rayleigh scattering—the same phenomenon that makes sunsets red and the sky blue. As sunlight passes through Earth's atmosphere, short blue wavelengths scatter, leaving red light to bend around our planet and reach the moon.
The August full moon, traditionally called the Sturgeon Moon by Native American tribes such as the Algonquin, marked the season when giant sturgeon were easily caught in the Great Lakes.

During the eclipse, the Moon Illusion (a trick of perception) makes the rising moon seem larger near the horizon. The event coincides with Raksha Bandhan, a Hindu festival celebrating sibling bonds with protective threads.

From the Americas to Africa, spectators will see up to 96% of the moon submerged in Earth's umbra—the darkest part of its shadow—peaking early on August 28. This celestial convergence offers a rare blend of science, culture, and natural beauty.

perspectives.description: This eclipse offers a free, accessible spectacle that can spark curiosity about astronomy and unite people across continents in shared awe of nature.
Light pollution, cloudy weather, or geographic limitations could obscure the view for many, and some communities might still attach unfounded superstitions to blood moons.
Eclipses are predictable celestial mechanics governed by orbital patterns, reminding us of the clockwork precision of our solar system and the value of scientific prediction.
Future eclipses will continue to provide opportunities for citizen science and public engagement with astronomy, potentially inspiring the next generation of scientists.
